R01-D-01: A familiar answer to the question of why citizens owe obedience to their state is that they have agreed to it. Few of us, of course, ever signed anything, so the agreement is said to be tacit: by continuing to live within a country's borders, using its roads and accepting the protection of its courts, a person signals consent to its authority. The view is attractive because it seems to reconcile two things that are otherwise difficult to hold together, allowing us to say that political authority is genuinely binding while also maintaining that no one is bound against their will, since anyone who objects remains free to leave. The trouble lies in that word 'free'. We do not normally count a choice as consent unless the person had a real alternative that could be taken at a bearable cost. Imagine a mining town with a single employer that also owns every shop, and suppose the company announces that anyone who keeps buying bread at its counters has thereby accepted all of its rules. No one would treat the purchase of bread as agreement, because the only way to refuse is to give up eating or to give up the town. Leaving a country is usually costlier still: it can mean abandoning one's language, one's family, one's work and the only place one knows well. There is, moreover, a further difficulty: almost every habitable stretch of the earth is now claimed by some state, so the emigrant does not escape political authority at all. She merely exchanges one authority for another, if another will admit her. The option on offer is not freedom from rule but the choice of a ruler. Defenders of the view have a reasonable reply. Consent, they say, comes in degrees, and the availability of exit is not nothing. A state that lets its citizens leave, and lets them take their savings with them, really does treat them differently from one that seals its borders, and it seems right to say that the first has a stronger claim on their loyalty. This should be granted. A right of exit is a genuine good, and a state that denies it has failed one important test of legitimacy. But to grant this is not to rescue the theory. That free exit is a condition of legitimacy does not make it the source of legitimacy, any more than an unlocked door makes a house a home. If a state's authority over those who stay can be justified, the justification must come from what the state does for and to them: whether its laws are fairly made, whether its burdens are fairly shared, whether its protection is extended to all. The language of tacit consent tends to obscure this question, since it allows a state to take credit for the mere fact that people have not fled, and to treat the absence of an escape as though it were an act of agreement.
R01-D-02: It is often said that a tolerant society is one in which people do not mind how others live, but this gets the idea almost exactly backwards. To tolerate something is to put up with it, and one can only put up with what one dislikes or disapproves of. A person who is untroubled by her neighbour's choice of diet, dress or companions is not tolerating that choice; she is simply indifferent to it, and indifference requires no effort and earns no praise. Toleration begins where objection begins: it is the decision not to act against something that one continues to regard as mistaken. Put this way, toleration can look puzzling, even paradoxical. If I believe that a practice is wrong, how can it be a virtue for me to let it continue? Surely the better person would either stop objecting or start resisting. The puzzle dissolves, however, once we recognise that the tolerant person holds reasons at two distinct levels. At the first level she objects to the practice; at the second level she has reasons, which she judges to be weightier, for not interfering with it: that adults have authority over their own lives, that her own judgement might be wrong, that a society in which everyone enforced their disapproval on everyone else would be unbearable. Consider a mother who thinks her grown son's choice of career foolish and tells him so, but would never dream of threatening to cut him out of her will to force him back. She has not abandoned her objection. She has ranked it beneath something she values more. Toleration so understood has limits, and they follow from the same structure. Where the second-level reasons give out, as when a practice inflicts harm on people who have not agreed to bear it, the case for restraint weakens and may disappear. A tolerant society is not one that permits everything. Some critics find the whole idea condescending: to be tolerated, they point out, is to be told that one is disapproved of and merely endured, and they propose that a just society should aim higher, at the positive recognition and affirmation of different ways of life. There is something in this complaint, since nobody enjoys being put up with. Yet the modesty of toleration is also its strength. It asks citizens who disagree deeply to share a political life without first requiring them to approve of one another, which is fortunate, because in a diverse society such approval is not going to be forthcoming. A demand for universal affirmation sounds more generous, but it may ask for what people cannot sincerely give.
R01-D-03: Theories of punishment have long been divided between those that look forward and those that look back. Forward-looking theories justify punishment by its effects: it deters, it incapacitates, perhaps it reforms. Their persistent embarrassment is that they seem to license too much. If the point of punishment were simply to discourage crime, then punishing an innocent person whom the public believed guilty might serve that point as well as punishing the guilty one, and sometimes better, since it would be quicker. Most people regard this conclusion as monstrous, which suggests that the effects of punishment, however important, cannot be the whole of its justification. An expressive theory offers to supply what is missing. On this view punishment is, before anything else, a form of communication: the community's way of declaring that an act was wrong and that the person who did it is answerable for it. This explains at once why the innocent may not be punished. To condemn someone who did nothing is not an inefficient use of punishment but a lie told in its language. It also explains why we distinguish a fine from a tax, though both take money: the tax carries no message of blame, while the fine carries little else. The obvious objection is that condemnation can be expressed in words. If the point of a prison sentence is to say that an act was wrong, why not simply say so, in a formal judgement solemnly delivered? The expressive theorist's reply is that words alone are too cheap to carry the message. A declaration that costs the offender nothing would be heard as a declaration that the wrong did not matter much; only something that is felt as a burden registers the seriousness of what was done. This reply is ingenious, but it has an uncomfortable implication. If hard treatment communicates because of the meanings a society attaches to it, then how much hard treatment is needed depends on those meanings, and meanings can drift. A society accustomed to long sentences will hear a short one as a shrug; the same sentence elsewhere might sound like thunder. The expressive theory, in other words, cannot by itself tell us how severe punishment should be, because severity is fixed by convention, and conventions can escalate without limit. That is not a reason to abandon the theory, which captures something the forward-looking view plainly misses. It is a reason to think that the theory needs a partner: some independent principle, perhaps of proportion or of humanity, that sets limits the language of condemnation cannot set for itself.
R01-D-04: The defence of meritocracy rests on a simple and appealing idea: that positions and rewards should go to those who earn them, through talent and effort, rather than to those born into the right family. Against the background of aristocratic privilege this was a revolutionary thought, and it remains a powerful one. Yet it has been attacked, with increasing force, on the ground that talent and effort are themselves largely matters of luck. No one chooses the abilities they are born with. And the capacity to work hard, to persist through failure and to defer gratification, is shaped by upbringing, health and circumstance in ways that no one controls. If this is so, the critic concludes, nobody deserves the rewards that meritocracy hands out, and the language of merit is a flattering fiction. The premises of this argument are difficult to deny, but its conclusion moves too fast. It runs together two different claims that a person might make about a reward. One is that she deserves it in a deep moral sense, that the world would be unjust if she did not have it. The other is that she is entitled to it, because she has met the conditions that a fair set of rules laid down in advance. A runner who wins a race under fair conditions is entitled to the prize even if her speed owes much to her genes and her coaching; to take the prize away on the ground that she was lucky would itself be a wrong, because she trained and competed on the understanding that winning would bring it. Entitlement of this kind does not depend on the winner being the author of her own talents. It depends only on the fairness of the rules and her compliance with them. Seen in this light, a society can reward productive contributions, and honour the expectations its rules create, without pretending that the rewards measure the moral worth of those who receive them. It also leaves open, as it should, the question of whether the rules themselves are fair, including how much inequality of reward they ought to permit. What the luck argument undermines is not the practice of rewarding achievement but a particular story told about it, the story in which the successful have simply earned their place and the unsuccessful have simply failed to earn theirs. That story is corrosive. It encourages the winners to regard their advantages as wholly their own, and it adds to the losers' material disadvantage the further injury of being told that they deserved it. The remedy is not to abolish merit but to hold it more lightly.
R01-D-05: In a society whose members hold different and often incompatible views about the meaning of life and the sources of value, on what basis may some of them use the power of the state to make others comply with laws? One influential answer holds that coercive laws must be justifiable by reasons that all reasonable citizens could accept, whatever their wider convictions. A law defended solely by appeal to a doctrine that many of one's fellow citizens reject, whether that doctrine is religious or secular, treats them as subjects to be managed rather than as equals to be persuaded. The requirement to offer such shared, or public, reasons is usually called the ideal of public reason. Critics have objected that the ideal asks too much of ordinary citizens. People do not keep their deepest convictions in a compartment separate from their political views; for many, their sense of what justice requires flows directly from a philosophical or religious outlook. To tell such citizens that they may vote, campaign and argue only on grounds detachable from that outlook is to ask them to enter public life as strangers to themselves. Worse, the demand seems to fall unevenly, since those whose convictions already happen to resemble the shared vocabulary are asked to give up nothing. Much of this objection depends on reading the ideal as a rule about what citizens may say. It is more plausible to read it as a test that laws must pass. On this reading a citizen may give whatever reasons move her, in the street, in the press or in the voting booth, and the ideal is satisfied so long as the law that is eventually enacted can also be supported by reasons that do not depend on any one contested doctrine. The burden then falls most heavily on those who exercise official power, on legislators drafting statutes and judges explaining decisions, rather than on citizens in conversation with one another. This reading does not remove every difficulty. If a citizen offers public reasons she does not herself find convincing, merely because she knows they are the only reasons that will count, her contribution begins to look less like persuasion and more like strategy. The ideal was meant to express respect for others as fellow reasoners, and insincere argument is a poor vehicle for respect. But this worry, though real, tells against a particular style of advocacy rather than against the test itself. A law can be justified in shared terms even if some of its supporters were moved by other considerations, just as a bridge can be sound though some of those who voted to build it understood nothing of engineering.
R01-D-06: The case for deciding by majority is usually made on grounds of fairness rather than wisdom. Majorities are not reliably right, but a procedure that counts each vote equally treats each voter as an equal, and no rival procedure seems to do so as well. There is a second, less often stated part of the case. Majority rule is tolerable to those who lose because losing is expected to be temporary. Today's minority may be tomorrow's majority, since coalitions shift as issues change, and a citizen who is outvoted on one question can reasonably expect to be on the winning side of another. Over time, the losses are spread around. This second condition does not always hold. When the issues that matter most to people line up with a stable division in the society, by language, region or ancestry, for instance, the same group may find itself outvoted on question after question for generations. Its members cast their votes, and their votes are counted equally, but the counting never changes the result. Formal equality at the ballot box then coexists with something very like permanent exclusion. To tell such a minority that it has been treated fairly because each of its votes weighed as much as anyone else's is to mistake the form of fairness for its substance. Various remedies have been proposed: requirements of supermajorities for certain decisions, the devolution of some powers to regions where the minority is concentrated, electoral systems that give smaller groups a share of seats, and constitutional rights that no majority may override. Each has costs. Supermajority rules protect minorities by making change difficult, which also protects whatever injustices the status quo contains. Devolution can create new minorities within the regions it empowers. Entrenched rights shift power from elected bodies to courts, whose members the minority usually has no means of holding to account. None of these costs settles the matter, but together they suggest that the problem should be framed differently. The persistent minority is not evidence that majority rule is unjust in itself. It is evidence that one of the conditions under which majority rule is fair has failed. The aim of a remedy, accordingly, should be to restore that condition where possible, for example by encouraging cross-cutting associations that loosen the grip of a single division on political life, rather than to replace majority rule with a different principle of decision. Where the condition cannot be restored, stronger protections may be needed, but they should be understood as repairs to a damaged procedure, not as a rival theory of legitimacy.
R01-D-07: For much of modern political thought, to be free has meant to be left alone. On this view a person's liberty is diminished whenever someone interferes with her choices, by force, by threat or by the closing off of options, and it is enlarged whenever such interference is removed. The view has the merit of simplicity, and it gives a clear direction to political argument: other things being equal, less interference means more freedom. An older tradition, recently revived, holds that this account misses something essential. What makes a person unfree, it says, is not interference as such but dependence on the will of another who could interfere at pleasure, whether or not he ever does. The point is easiest to see in a case where the two accounts come apart. Imagine a tenant whose lease allows the landlord to evict her at any time and for any reason, and whose landlord happens to be a mild man who has never troubled anyone. On the non-interference view the tenant is perfectly free, since nobody is stopping her from doing anything. Yet she knows her position. She will think twice before complaining about a broken boiler, she will keep her opinion of the landlord to herself, and she may find herself anticipating his preferences in matters he has never raised. The absence of interference in her life is not evidence that she is free; it may be, in part, an effect of her unfreedom, since a person who must stay in another's good graces learns to make interference unnecessary. The rival tradition calls her condition domination, and it defines freedom as the absence of domination. The shift has striking consequences. Interference, on this view, does not always reduce freedom. A law that restrains me, but that I and others like me can contest through courts, elections and other channels that force those who make it to take our interests into account, does not subject me to anyone's arbitrary will, and so does not make me less free, even though it limits what I may do. Conversely, a benevolent ruler who chooses to interfere very little may still leave his subjects unfree, because what they are permitted to do depends on his continued goodwill. Critics reply that the notion of arbitrary power is too elastic to do the work asked of it. Almost every relationship, from employment to marriage to the ordinary dealings of neighbours, contains some capacity of one party to make the other's life worse. If all such capacities count as domination, then domination is everywhere and the concept loses its edge; if only some do, we need a criterion, and the obvious candidates seem to smuggle back the very judgements about interference that the theory hoped to avoid. Defenders answer that power is arbitrary when it is not forced to track the interests of those subject to it, and that whether it is so forced is a question about institutions: about rights of exit, of appeal and of collective voice. This answer is better than the critics allow, but it is not quite enough to turn non-domination into a measure. It tells us where to look rather than how much freedom we will find there. That may be its real value. The non-interference view, by counting acts, trains attention on what happens; the rival view, by asking about standing, trains it on what could happen, and on the structures that make some things unthinkable to attempt. Even if it cannot yield a neat scale, the second view identifies a kind of unfreedom that a tally of interferences would never register.
R01-D-08: Egalitarians hold that there is something wrong with inequality as such: that when some people are much worse off than others through no fault of their own, the situation is bad, and bad in part simply because of the gap. The most famous objection to this view asks us to consider what follows from it. Suppose that the only way to remove an inequality were to make the better off worse off, with no benefit to anyone, as if a town in which some households had gardens and others had none could reach equality only by paving over every garden. If inequality is bad in itself, then such a change would remove something bad, and so would be in one respect an improvement. Yet the change helps no one and harms many. To call it an improvement in any respect, the objectors say, is absurd. Many philosophers have been moved by this objection to give up equality as a fundamental value. Some have adopted the view that benefits matter more the worse off their recipient is, so that a gain to a poor person counts for more than the same gain to a rich one; others hold that what matters is that everyone should have enough, after which differences cease to be of moral concern. Neither view is troubled by levelling down, since on neither does reducing the well-being of the better off, by itself, improve anything. Both also capture much of what drew people to equality in the first place, which was a concern for those who are badly off. Yet the objection is less decisive than it is usually taken to be. The egalitarian need not claim that a levelled-down world is better all things considered, only that it is better in one respect while much worse in others. Plural values often pull apart in this way. We can think that a promise kept at terrible cost was in one respect admirable without thinking that it should have been kept. Seen this way, the levelling-down case shows only that equality is not the only thing that matters, which almost no egalitarian ever believed. This defence succeeds, but at a price. It keeps equality as a value only by making it a strangely impersonal one: something that can make a state of affairs better while making it better for no one at all. Many will find such a value hard to care about. There is, however, another way to understand what egalitarians were after. On a relational view, the core of equality lies not in how goods are distributed but in how people stand to one another: in the absence of rank, servility and contempt, in a society where no one must bow and no one may command another merely by virtue of birth or wealth. Inequalities of resources matter on this view chiefly because, beyond some point, they turn into inequalities of standing, as when wealth buys influence over others or poverty forces deference to them. The relational view is untouched by the levelling-down objection, because paving over gardens neither creates nor abolishes any relation of rank between neighbours. Whether it can say enough about distribution is a further question. A society might abolish titles and deference while leaving vast differences in income intact, and the relational egalitarian owes us an account of when such differences begin to corrode equal standing. But the view has at least located the value of equality in a relation between persons, which is where most of its defenders always felt it to be.
